paragraphs.text: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type 3 (FHH3) is an autosomal dominant disorder of extracellular calcium homeostasis affecting the parathyroids, kidneys, and bone. Like FHH1 and FHH2, it is characterized by lifelong elevation of serum calcium with inappropriately low urinary calcium excretion, but FHH3 has distinctive features that include increased serum PTH concentrations, hypophosphatemia, and osteomalacia (Nesbit et al., 2013). Howles et al. (2016) described FHH3 as the most severe of the 3 variants clinically.

checks.evidence_quote: FHH3, together with FHH1 and FHH2 are genetically heterogenous autosomal dominant disorders of extracellular-calcium (Cao2+) homeostasis

paragraphs.text: McMurtry et al. (1992) described a large kindred with familial benign hypercalcemia in which 46 members spanning 5 generations, aged 1.5 to 91 years, were surveyed biochemically and/or by chart review; 19 were affected. In the 15 hypercalcemic subjects examined biochemically, serum immunoreactive PTH levels, measured in 3 separate immunoassays, became supranormal by about age 30 years and appeared to increase further thereafter. Serum alkaline phosphatase and creatinine were normal, but inorganic phosphate levels were lower than in unaffected kindred members. Three of 5 affected adults older than 40 years who were studied radiographically had changes suggestive of osteomalacia, and iliac crest biopsy after tetracycline labeling in a 51-year-old woman confirmed defective skeletal mineralization. The authors concluded that the disorder may not be totally benign and that osteomalacia, perhaps due to mild hypophosphatemia, can develop in adulthood.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2010) reported a second FHH3 kindred. The proband, a 43-year-old woman without a CASR mutation in the coding region or splice sites, presented with a corrected serum calcium of 2.74 mmol/liter (normal, 2.15-2.55), serum PTH of 47 pg/ml (normal, 10-65), and a urinary calcium clearance:creatinine clearance ratio of 0.006. Of 24 members from 3 generations of her kindred, 16 were hypercalcemic with normal or elevated serum PTH and mild hypophosphatemia, features consistent with FHH3.

paragraphs.text: Fujisawa et al. (2013) reported a Japanese female infant found to have hypercalcemia on routine testing for poor weight gain on breast feeding. At 49 days of age, serum calcium (adjusted by Payne's formula) was 13.1 mg/dL, intact PTH 27 pg/mL, and urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio 1.29 mg/mg. There was no evidence of hyperparathyroidism, PTHrP-producing neoplasm, or vitamin D excess. Thus, unlike typical FHH, the infant had hypercalciuria.

paragraphs.text: Howles et al. (2016) reported 3 unrelated probands with FHH3. A 34-year-old woman with a 12-year history of hypercalcemia presented with fatigue, headaches, and persistent generalized aches that did not resolve after parathyroidectomy; a 22-year-old man presented with hypercalcemia, fatigue, and generalized rib pain; and a 52-year-old woman with an approximately 20-year history of hypercalcemia presented with headaches, abdominal pain, vomiting, fatigue, and musculoskeletal pain that did not resolve after pamidronate infusion or parathyroidectomy.

paragraphs.text: Hannan et al. (2010) refined the FBHH3 locus with 24 polymorphic loci (17 microsatellites and 7 SNPs) in 34 members from 5 generations of the Oklahoma kindred (19 affected). The peak lod score was 6.92 at 0% recombination with D19S606, and recombinants placed FBHH3 in a 4.1-Mb interval flanked by D19S112 and rs245111. The syntenic region on mouse chromosome 7 contains 4 Casr-related sequences (Gprc2a-rs), but human homologs were not found; comparative analysis showed loss from the human genome of an 11.6-Mb region containing these 4 sequences. Sequencing of the coding regions and intron-exon boundaries of 12 other candidate genes from the interval that are expressed in parathyroid and/or kidney found no abnormalities in an affected individual.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in an affected member of each of the 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds (the Oklahoma kindred and the kindred reported by Nesbit et al., 2010). Analysis of variants within the 3.46-Mbp 19q13.3 interval identified in both patients a single variant, a C-to-T transition in exon 2 of the AP2S1 gene predicting an arg15-to-cys (R15C) substitution. The change was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and restriction enzyme analysis showed cosegregation in members (reported as 32 affected and 23 unaffected) from 4 generations of the 2 kindreds. Sequencing of AP2S1 in 50 unrelated FHH patients in whom CASR mutations had been excluded identified 11 heterozygous missense mutations, all affecting arg15: 4 R15C, 3 arg15-to-his (R15H), and 4 arg15-to-leu (R15L). Arg15 is conserved in AP2-sigma-2 orthologs and in human AP sigma subunit paralogs, and the authors estimated that AP2S1 Arg15 mutations may underlie FHH in more than 20% of patients without CASR mutations. In HEK293 cells stably expressing CASR, all 3 mutants shifted the concentration-response curves to extracellular calcium to the right, with significantly higher EC50 values than wildtype, indicating decreased sensitivity to extracellular calcium; the R15C mutant gave an EC50 significantly higher than vector alone, suggesting a possible dominant-negative effect. Following calcium stimulation, cells transfected with R15C had less reduction in cell-surface CASR than cells transfected with wildtype AP2S1, indicating reduced CASR endocytosis. Removal of the C-terminal CASR dileucine motif also decreased cellular sensitivity to extracellular calcium.

agent.process_note: I read all 8 papers. Five are abstracts only (McMurtry 1992, Trump 1995, Lloyd 1999, Nesbit 2010, Fujisawa 2013). Three are full texts: Hannan 2010, Nesbit 2013 and Howles 2016. Nesbit 2013 gives nucleotide changes only as codon changes (the Arg15Cys entry in its Table 1 reads 'CGC→TTGC', which looks like a typo) and gives no c.-numbering, so the HGVS field uses protein names. Its count of family members tested for cosegregation differs between the main text (32 affected, 23 unaffected) and the methods (17+15 in one kindred and 16+7 in the other); I reported the main-text figures. The reference data gave no MIM number or cytogenetic location for AP2S1, so the intro uses 19q13, the locus location from the papers, and gives no gene MIM number. The papers do not state the ancestry of the second (FHHNI) kindred, so I did not state it.
